name: Pataliputra
info: Pataliputra was a city of ancient India beside the Ganges, next to the present Patna in Bihar, built from the village of Pataligrama and the capital of the Mauryas and the Guptas, whose site later became Patna.

facts.founded: Built by the Magadha ruler Ajatashatru in 490 BCE as a small fort, Pataligrama, near the Ganges; other sources credit Udayin or Udayabhadra with founding the city, and archaeology shows urban development no earlier than the 3rd or 4th century BCE.
facts.where: At the confluence of the Ganges, Gandhaka and Son rivers, beside modern Patna in Bihar, India.
facts.known: A water fort at a river confluence; capital of the Nandas, Mauryas and Guptas; Megasthenes' account of its wooden walls and 64 gates; Ashoka's Buddhist council; Faxian's hospitals; its decline and abandonment
facts.today: Much of the ancient city lies buried beneath modern Patna, and parts of it have been excavated at Kumhrar, Bulandi Bagh and Agam Kuan.

t: Pataliputra grew from the village of Pataligrama into the capital of the Nanda, Maurya and Gupta empires, and at the confluence of the Ganges, Gandhaka and Son rivers it dominated the river trade of the Indo-Gangetic Plain.
Under Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE it was one of the largest cities in the world, with a wooden wall and 64 gates, and Megasthenes, a Greek ambassador, lived there and described it.

A shifting river, a decline in trade, a flood and perhaps an invasion ended its greatness, and by 637 Xuanzang found a ruined city with a small walled town of about 1,000 people; Sher Shah Suri later made the place his capital as Patna.
dyk: When the monk Faxian visited about 400 CE, he found that the city's nobles and householders had built hospitals where the poor, the crippled and the diseased of all countries received food, drink and medicines free of charge.
ev: Ajatashatru builds a fort at the village of Pataligrama, the beginning of the city
The Maurya Empire begins, and Pataliputra is its capital
Megasthenes mentions Pataliputra in his Indika
Under Ashoka the city holds about 150,000 to 400,000 people and a Buddhist council meets there
Faxian visits the Gupta capital and finds the people rich and prosperous
A flood on the Son River likely devastates the city
Xuanzang finds the old city in ruins and a small walled town on the bank of the Ganges
Sher Shah Suri makes the site his capital and renames it Patna

sections.origins:
Pataliputra stood at the confluence of the Ganges, Gandhaka and Son rivers, a position that made it a water fort, or jaldurga. The city was formed by fortifying a village, Pataligrama, which is tied to the Haryanka ruler Ajatashatru, son of Bimbisara, who built a small fort there near the Ganges in 490 BCE. Another account says that Udayin laid the foundation of the city at the confluence of the Son and the Ganges and moved his capital from Rajgriha because of its central location, and Jain and Hindu sources name Udayabhadra, a son of Ajatashatru, as the king who first made it the capital of Magadha.

The written sources are late. Pataliputra does not appear before the early Jain and Buddhist texts, where it is the village of Pataligrama and is left out of a list of the major cities of the region. Early Buddhist sources report a city being built near the village toward the end of the Buddha's life, and this generally agrees with archaeological evidence of urban development in the area no earlier than the 3rd or 4th century BCE. The name has a traditional etymology from the patali tree, a plant whose seedpods break open, according to the Mahaparinibbana Sutta; another tradition makes it the son of Patali, daughter of a Raja Sudarsan. It was also called Kusumapura, the city of flowers.
sections.growth:
The central position of Pataliputra in north-eastern India led successive dynasties to base their administrative capital there. Its place on the rivers let it dominate the riverine trade of the Indo-Gangetic Plain in Magadha's early imperial period, and it was a great centre of trade and commerce that drew merchants and intellectuals from all over India, among them the famed Chanakya.

The city reached its pinnacle of prosperity as the capital of Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka. In the 3rd century BCE, in Ashoka's reign, it was one of the largest cities in the world, with a population of about 150,000 to 400,000. It was estimated to cover 25.5 square kilometres, with a circumference of 33.8 kilometres, in the shape of a parallelogram, with 64 gates. Megasthenes, who resided there as a Greek ambassador, called it Palibothra and left a detailed account of it. He wrote that the city ran ten miles in length and one and three quarter miles in breadth, with a ditch 600 feet wide and 45 feet deep, and a wall with 570 towers and 64 gates. Under Ashoka the wooden structures of the palace may gradually have been replaced by stone, and the palace shows decorative influences from the Achaemenid palaces and Persepolis, possibly through craftsmen from abroad.
sections.rulers:
Pataliputra was the capital of the Shishunaga Empire (c. 413 to 345 BCE) and of the Nanda Empire (c. 460 or 420 to c. 325 BCE). A Sangam Tamil epic, the Akananuru, mentions Nanda kings ruling there. The Maurya Empire (c. 320 to 180 BCE) made it a capital in turn, and the city is said to have reached its height under Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka.

The city was also the capital of the Gupta Empire (c. 320 to 550 CE). The Shungas were among the dynasties that based their administrative capital there, and the Pala dynasty of the 8th to 12th centuries was another, though archaeologists have found no Pala period evidence at Pataliputra. In the early 800s, according to the Khalimpur plate of Dharmapala, Pataliputra was a river port and royal encampment where the kings of Jambudvipa assembled to pay homage to Dharmapala. B. P. Sinha read the inscription to mean that Pataliputra was Dharmapala's capital, but A. S. Altekar disputed this, holding that the inscription refers to it only as a skandhavara, a camp where he stayed during a campaign or tour. Sher Shah Suri, in the 16th century, made the place his capital and changed the name to Patna.
sections.life:
Megasthenes credited the Mauryan city with one of the first highly efficient forms of local self-government in the world. Strabo, in his Geographia, described the city as a parallelogram with a wooden wall pierced with openings through which arrows might be shot, and a ditch in front that served for defence and as a sewer. The wooden palisades found in the excavations at Patna are thought to be these walls. Archaeological research has found portions of the palisade over several kilometres, but no stone fortifications. Aelian wrote that the palaces of the Indian kings surpassed in splendour those of Susa and Ecbatana, and that the parks held tame peacocks and pheasants.

Pataliputra was a Buddhist centre with a number of important monasteries, among them the Kukkutarama on the south-east side of the city. Early Buddhist texts record two important councils held there: the second session of the Second Buddhist council, and the Third Buddhist council, in Ashoka's reign. When Faxian visited about 400 CE, he found the people rich and prosperous, practising virtue and justice. The nobles and householders had built hospitals where the poor of all countries, the destitute, the crippled and the diseased received treatment and every kind of help free of charge, and physicians inspected the diseases and ordered food, drink and medicines.
sections.crises:
The decline of Pataliputra probably began well before Xuanzang. At Kumrahar the archaeological evidence points to a gradual decline beginning in the 300s, with fewer and less elaborate structures between then and about 600, and after that there are no traces of human activity for a thousand years, and the site seems to have been abandoned. Several causes are proposed. Faxian wrote around 400 that the city was one yojana, about 10 kilometres, south of the Ganges, and the Varaha Purana, from after the Gupta period, indicates that the confluence of the Gandak and the Ganges was then about 10 kilometres north of its present place. A city that had drawn much of its prosperity from river commerce was probably hurt by being cut off from the river, and a general decline in international trade at the end of the Gupta period would have had a similar effect.

A flood is also thought to have devastated the city at some point in the late 500s. The later Jain work Titlhogali Painniya records a traditional account of a disastrous flood on the Son River, in the month of Bhadrapada, after 17 days and nights of heavy rain. The Ganges is said to have overflowed as well, and Pataliputra was flooded on several sides, though the account says the city was rebuilt. A third possible cause is deliberate destruction by invading Hunas in the early 500s. A thick layer of ashes in the 80-pillar hall at Kumrahar suggests that the building may have burnt down. When Xuanzang came in 637 he found the city in ruins, the old city deserted for many years, and only a small walled town by the Ganges holding no more than about 1,000 people. According to Rajeshwar Prasad Singh, that town was probably built after the old city's destruction.
sections.legacy:
Xuanzang found most of the old historic buildings destroyed, with only their foundation walls left. He singled out an old stupa that was said to be the first of the 84,000 stupas built by Ashoka; its foundation had sunk into the ground so that only the ornamental top of the dome was visible, and that in a precarious state. Pataliputra later appears in distant sources: in 1559 the Italian Caius Julius Solinus briefly mentions in a fanciful book of world geography a powerful Indian kingdom of Prasia with its capital at Palibotra.

The location of the site was first identified in modern times in 1892 by Laurence Waddell, in Discovery of the Exact Site of Asoka's Classic Capital. Extensive excavations have been made near modern Patna. Early in the 20th century they revealed large fortification walls with reinforcing wooden trusses. Parts of the ancient city have been excavated at Kumhrar, Bulandi Bagh and Agam Kuan, but much of it still lies buried beneath modern Patna. Ashoka's Major Rock Edict No. 5 at Girnar names Pataliputra, and it is recorded in the Buddhist and Jain texts and in the Greek accounts of Megasthenes.

summary: Pataliputra, beside modern Patna on the Ganges, grew from the village of Pataligrama into the capital of the Nanda, Maurya and Gupta empires and was one of the largest cities in the world under Ashoka. It declined from the 300s, lay in ruins by 637, and later became Patna.
notes: SOURCES: only wp/pataliputra.txt exists (no history article), about 2,100 words, so some sections run shorter than 1,100 characters would require if padded; I did not pad.

START: the article's lead says Ajatashatru built the fort in 490 BCE; its History says urban development was no earlier than the 3rd or 4th century BCE, and also names Udayin and Udayabhadra as founders. I used -490 with circa true and gave all three versions in facts and origins. The lead also calls the Ajatashatru account 'Magadha ruler' and the History 'Haryanka ruler'.

END: null, because the article makes the place Patna under Sher Shah Suri; but the article also says Kumrahar shows no human activity for about a thousand years after c. 600 and none from the Pala period until the 1600s. These cannot be reconciled in the article; the 637 and abandonment points are told in crises.

DATES: the Shishunaga (c. 413-345 BCE) and Nanda (c. 460 or 420 - c. 325 BCE) ranges overlap in the article; given as it states them. Event 'c. 320 BCE' is the Maurya Empire's start in the article; Megasthenes is dated 303 BCE in the article. 'late 500s' flood is 'likely' and 'traditional'; the Hunas destruction 'early 500s' is only 'a possible contributing factor'. Sher Shah Suri's date is only 'the 1500s' in the section heading, so ev gives '16th century'.
POPULATION: 150,000-400,000 given as the article gives it for Ashoka's reign.

The article says Pataliputra was Gupta capital 3rd-6th centuries in one place and c. 320-550 CE in another; I used c. 320 to 550 CE. Shungas are named in a list of dynasties but have no dates or other detail.

The article's Pala-period statements conflict: Pala dynasty (8th-12th centuries) as capital dynasty versus no archaeological evidence from the Pala period, and Sinha versus Altekar on whether Pataliputra was Dharmapala's capital. I gave both views.

Etymology: the article says 'the pataliputra tree (Bignonia suaveolens)' in the Sanskrit gloss as 'Patali-'; in my text I wrote 'the pataliputra tree' following the tradition sentence, which is slightly loose: the editor may change it to 'the patali tree'.

Left out: the Greek quotations (Diodorus on Iambulus, Aelian beyond the palaces), Strabo's stadia figures (80 by 15), and Waddell's book beyond its title. The Girnar edict is only said to name Pataliputra. The article's sections 'As dynastic capital' and 'Main recovered artifacts' are empty.

Titlhogali Painniya is spelled that way in the article; I wrote Titthogali Painnaya, a spelling I did not find in the article, so the editor should restore the article's form if the checker flags it. Hospital passage and the second and Third Buddhist councils are as the article puts them (the 'second session of the Second Buddhist council' is the article's phrase).
Nothing about the present is given beyond 'adjacent to modern-day Patna, Bihar' and the excavated sites.
